name: Prior Art and Clearance Searching
title: Prior Art and Clearance Searching
answer: Prior art and clearance searching covers two related but distinct jobs. Prior art searching looks for patents, published applications, technical papers, products, and public disclosures that predate a claimed invention, to assess patentability or validity. Clearance searching, sometimes called freedom to operate or trademark clearance, checks whether a proposed product, name, or mark would infringe existing rights. The work spans patents, trademarks, designs, and sometimes copyright, and it happens before filing, before launch, and before investment. It is a core part of intellectual property strategy and a routine task for patent agents, trademark attorneys, and search professionals.

sections.body: Prior art and clearance searching covers two related but distinct jobs. Prior art searching looks for patents, published applications, technical papers, products, and public disclosures that predate a claimed invention, to assess patentability or validity. Clearance searching, sometimes called freedom to operate or trademark clearance, checks whether a proposed product, name, or mark would infringe existing rights. The work spans patents, trademarks, designs, and sometimes copyright, and it happens before filing, before launch, and before investment. It is a core part of intellectual property strategy and a routine task for patent agents, trademark attorneys, and search professionals.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on large public and commercial databases. Patent offices such as the USPTO, the EPO, and WIPO provide bulk data, full text, and classification schemes like the CPC and IPC. Trademark registers, company registries, domain records, and non-patent literature collections add further sources. Modern search platforms use Boolean and proximity operators, and increasingly they use vector search, embeddings, and machine learning to rank results. The infrastructure also includes document delivery, translation services, and audit logs that record what was searched and when.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A search begins with a clear definition of the invention or the mark, often built from claim language, product specifications, or brand usage. The searcher develops keywords, synonyms, classifications, and search strings, then runs them across the chosen databases. Results are reviewed for relevance, with close reads of claims, figures, and legal status. For clearance, the searcher checks registers for identical or similar marks, and also looks at common law use, domain names, and marketplace evidence. AI tools can help cluster results, translate foreign language documents, and flag near matches, but a human still decides what matters, and the output is usually a written report with charts, relevance ratings, and copies of key references.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk, and provenance shape how searches are done and how results are used. Confidentiality and privilege matter, because search requests can reveal product plans or legal strategy. Provenance means keeping a clear record of which databases were queried, which filters were applied, and which documents were reviewed, so the work can be defended later. Accuracy is critical, since a missed reference can lead to an invalid patent or an infringement claim. The site tracks 146 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which shows that IP disputes involving AI are active, and the site also tracks 29 AI case law precedents, a sign that courts are still shaping the rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more automation and more data. Search platforms are adding semantic search, large language models for summarization, and automated claim charting, which speeds up review but raises new questions about verification. Global patent and trademark offices are expanding their bulk data and machine-readable formats, making cross-jurisdiction searching easier. At the same time, the volume of AI-related filings and disputes is growing, so clearance work is likely to remain in demand. The core challenge will stay the same: finding the right references and proving that the search was thorough.
